body: Hey looks like we need to add a marker for RWKV-7 in conftest.py, I can take care of that to ensure tests run properly.

Thanks for offering!

I looked into this — I don't think a `conftest.py` marker is needed. The markers registered there are all functional categories (`slow`, `torch_export_test`, `flash_attn_test`, …); models aren't registered per-name, and the existing `rwkv` (RWKV-4) model isn't either.

The one place that does key off the name is `tests/generation/test_utils.py`, which checks `"rwkv" in model_class.__name__.lower()` — `Rwkv7ForCausalLM` already matches, so that skip fires correctly today. I see it in a local run of `tests/models/rwkv7/`:

```
SKIPPED [1] tests/generation/test_utils.py:505: Won't fix: model with non-standard dictionary output shapes
```

The tests do get collected — the CI fetcher picks up `tests/models/rwkv7/` from the changed files, and 304 tests collect locally. If you're seeing something that suggests otherwise, I'd genuinely like to know — happy to be wrong here.

If you're looking for something to pick up on RWKV-7, the PR itself (#47780) is the place that needs eyes.

Got it. Makes total sense—thanks for double-checking the test collection logic and test_utils.py.

I'll jump over to PR #47780 directly and take a look at the implementation/review there instead!

Thanks for this — the official checkpoints solve the packaging problem that got the earlier request (#46984) declined, so this is genuinely good news for the integration.

I checked compatibility against `RWKV/RWKV7-1.5B-20260805` just now, and the two efforts already line up:

- `Rwkv7Config` in #47780 accepts the official `config.json` unchanged — every key in it is a declared parameter of `Rwkv7Config`, except `model_type`, which the base class handles. (Checked against the declared signature rather than by construction, since `PretrainedConfig` would absorb unknown keys into `**kwargs`.)
- Reading the `model.safetensors` header directly: **798 tensors, exact name match and exact shape match against `Rwkv7ForCausalLM`'s state dict, zero mismatches.**

So #47780's modeling code loads these checkpoints as-is, with no changes needed on either side.

I'm happy to point the doc examples and the `configuration_rwkv7.py` docstring checkpoint at the official repos.

One thing I'd suggest keeping as-is: the slow integration test doesn't use any of my conversions — it downloads `BlinkDL/rwkv-7-world`'s raw 0.1B `.pth`, converts it, and compares against values produced by BlinkDL's own `rwkv` runtime rather than by this implementation. 0.1B is also deliberate: at 768 wide with head_dim 64 the head *count* (12) and head *width* (64) differ, so an index mix-up can't pass by coincidence — at 7.2B and 13.3B both are 64. The 1.5B would work for that (32 heads × 64) but re-anchoring would mean recomputing the expected values and a ~3 GB download per CI run, and I think the non-self-certifying property is worth more than the newer weights here.

@ArthurZucker @Cyrilvallez — #47780 is rebased, green, and loads these checkpoints unchanged. It's the natural base to build on.

Verified the official checkpoints against #47780 on 8×A800. Everything below is measured, not inferred.

## The release is a lossless re-packing of the source

`RWKV/RWKV7-1.5B-20260805` is byte-identical to `BlinkDL/rwkv7-g1`'s `rwkv7-g1i-1.5b-20260805-ctx16384.pth`: **798/798 tensors**, same `bf16` storage dtype, matched by content hash rather than by name — so no naming convention has to be agreed before the comparison means anything, and nothing of this implementation is in the loop.

(This also answers a question that came up separately: the safetensors conversion loses no precision. At equal storage dtype a faithful conversion *must* be bit-identical, so it is checkable rather than a matter of opinion.)

## It loads into #47780 unchanged

No conversion, no `trust_remote_code`. Every key in `config.json` is a declared parameter of `Rwkv7Config` except `model_type`, which the base class handles. 798 tensors match by name and by shape.

## Numerics, against BlinkDL's own numpy forward

The reference is `RWKV-v7/rwkv_v7_numpy.py`, not this implementation:

| check | result |
|---|---|
| fp32 greedy output, 24 lambada prompts | **24/24 identical** |
| batch invariance, b1 vs b4 and b1 vs b8 (fp32) | **0/24 differing** |
| left-padding invariance (fp32) | **0/8 differing** |
| state carry, incremental vs one-shot (fp32) | 1.9e-6 relative |
| state carry, 4096 tokens split vs whole (fp32) | 1.3e-6 relative |

bf16 differs on 2 of those 24 continuations. Both are near-ties: the first divergence is at generated token 9, where the top1−top2 margin is **0.023 logits** — several recurrent steps of an 8-bit mantissa are enough to tip that. The fp32 arm being exact is what identifies this as precision and not an implementation error; a bf16-only run could not distinguish the two.

`tests/models/rwkv7/`: **130 passed, 1583 subtests, 0 failed.**

## Changes pushed

The docs and the `configuration_rwkv7.py` docstring now point at the official repos, and the `trust_remote_code` line the World tokenizer used to need is gone — these repos ship the vocabulary as a `tokenizer.json`, so `AutoTokenizer` loads it as an ordinary fast tokenizer. The section that opened with "No checkpoint on the Hub loads into this implementation as-is" was true when written and is not any more, so it says what is true now.

The slow integration test is deliberately unchanged. It converts BlinkDL's raw 0.1B `.pth` and compares against values from BlinkDL's runtime, so it does not certify this implementation with this implementation; and at 768 wide the head count (12) and the head width (64) differ, so an index mix-up cannot pass by coincidence — a property no release at 1.5B or above provides, since 7.2B and 13.3B are 64 and 64.

@ArthurZucker @Cyrilvallez — #47780 is rebased, green, and loads these checkpoints as they are. Every number above is reproducible; happy to add any further check you want to see in the PR.
@Hakureirm if you have divergence with numpy it's mean you have casting/order issue, you are not supposed to have divergence with numpy implementation

The fp32 arm has no divergence — **24/24 identical** to the numpy reference. The 22/24 is the bf16 arm: our bf16 run against an fp32 reference, which is a precision comparison rather than an implementation one.

Your criterion is the right one, and it is exactly why both arms were run. A casting or ordering fault does not depend on mantissa width, so it would show in fp32 as well. It does not — and a bf16-only run could not have told the two explanations apart.

Quantified, from the same run:

- bf16↔fp32 logit deviation: **1.3e-2 relative** (median over 8 prompts × all positions; ~1.2 logits absolute at this scale, worst 2.1e-2).
- top1−top2 margin at the first flipped token: **0.023 logits**. The decision sits roughly **50× inside** that noise.
- the deviation is **unbiased**: mean signed deviation over mean |logit| is **+1.8e-4**, about 70× smaller than the deviation's own magnitude. A casting or ordering fault produces a biased offset; symmetric rounding is what this looks like.
- accumulated over 24 layers, √24 · 2⁻⁸ ≈ 1.9e-2, which is the band the measured 1.3e-2 falls in.

Two further checks since the previous comment, both prompted by asking what could still be wrong with it:

- the source→release tensor match is a **bijection** — 798 distinct content hashes on each side, zero collisions — so "798/798 byte-identical" is one-to-one and not several source tensors landing on one release tensor.
- the World tokenizer (`rwkv` package) and the HF fast tokenizer agree on **all 24 prompts**, so the reference run and ours saw identical token sequences. The earlier comparison was on decoded text, which had assumed this rather than shown it.

@Hakureirm thanks for the clarification. I initially understood the comparison as BF16 against BF16, not BF16 against an FP32 reference.

I agree that the two different continuations alone are not enough to claim an implementation bug.

My concern: the FP32 result cannot exclude an issue that only appears at the BF16/FP32 casting boundaries. In #47780 at commit `13aa2948`, the six recurrent inputs are cast to FP32 before the `value @ key` and anti-update products. In the published official PyTorch runtime, those products are formed in the activation dtype before the result is accumulated in FP32.

A clean FP32-vs-FP32 comparison does not exercise that difference, because the BF16 boundary is absent from both sides.

Your state-carry checks also show that the default `T > 1` and `T = 1` paths do not produce exactly identical recurrent states (`1.9e-6` and `1.3e-6` relative), even though the FP32 generated tokens remain identical. This does not prove a bug, and I am not attributing the difference only to chunking, since the projection shapes also differ between prefill and decode. It does mean that token equality alone is not enough to resolve the casting question.

The additional validation I am asking for this: BF16 against BF16 using the official runtime, with the same forced tokens, and a step-by-step comparison of logits and recurrent states?

Ran the validation you asked for: BF16 against BF16 using the official runtime,
same forced tokens, step-by-step logits and recurrent states. On an RTX 3090,
24 lambada prompts, both a `T>1` prefill leg and a `T=1` decode leg with each
implementation carrying its own state trajectory. The reference arm is the
`rwkv` package's pure-PyTorch path (`RWKV_V7_ON=1`, no CUDA kernel), weights
rebuilt from the official safetensors by prefix rename only — sound because the
release is a content-hash bijection of the source `.pth` (measured above) — and
verified bitwise after the rename. TF32 was disabled on both arms; pass/fail
criteria were fixed before the run.

**fp32 gate first** (a casting or ordering fault does not depend on mantissa
width, so the harness has to be clean there before bf16 numbers mean anything):
worst relative deviation across all logits positions and all 24 per-layer
states, both legs: **8.2e-6** — orders of magnitude below any top-1 margin, so
the earlier 24/24 result is subsumed by a stronger check on this harness.

**bf16-vs-bf16:**

- logits relative deviation, median: **9.8e-3** (prefill) / **5.9e-3** (decode);
  worst 4.1e-2. Below the √24·2⁻⁸ ≈ 1.9e-2 random-walk band — consistent with
  the two arms sharing most of their bf16 matmul rounding and differing mainly
  at the boundary in question.
- per-layer state deviation rises to ~9e-3 by layer 16 and saturates (no
  unbounded growth).
- **bias, the criterion your concern turns on** — measured on the state, which
  is the direct product of the `v⊗k` and anti-update products and sits before
  the GroupNorm that would launder any affine offset: additive component
  **5.9e-6**, scale-correlated component **4.4e-5**, i.e. 137× and 18× inside
  the alarm line of one tenth of the deviation magnitude. On logits: 2.9e-4,
  1/21 of the deviation (the fp32-era figure was 1/72). Symmetric rounding,
  no directional offset.
- **T>1 vs T=1**, where your reservation was exactly right: each arm's own
  one-shot-vs-stepwise state disagreement is **7.20e-3 (ours, chunked vs
  sequential)** and **7.08e-3 (official runtime, seq vs one)** — the same
  magnitude in an implementation that has no chunking at all. In our CPU
  self-check the official pair was bit-identical; on CUDA the `[T,C]` and
  `[1,C]` projection matmuls take different reduction orders. So the effect you declined to
  attribute solely to chunking is indeed dominated by the projection shapes,
  and it is shared, not ours.

Taken together: the BF16/FP32 casting-boundary difference between the two
implementations shows up as unbiased, saturating rounding noise, with no
systematic offset at the state level where those products actually live. It
does not provide evidence of an implementation error, and it fills the coverage
gap you correctly pointed out in the fp32-only comparison.

Harness (criteria fixed pre-run, probe self-checked against injected faults,
per-run path assertions) and both result JSONs are reproducible; happy to share
the scripts or add any further slice you want to see.
Will have a look ina bit!

Bf16 vs bf16 under same machine and bf16 checkpoints need to have exact state exact logits no deviation or its not the same implementation. The reference is RWKV-LM as it’s the trainer use by RWKV checkpoints

On the reference: RWKV-LM is what the fp32 comparison already used. The reference there was `RWKV-v7/rwkv_v7_numpy.py`, and in the 08-06 run above the fp32 greedy output matched it on 24/24 lambada prompts. The bf16 leg used BlinkDL's `rwkv` package because the request was for the official runtime specifically. If you want a particular RWKV-LM script in that leg as well, name it and I will add it.

On bitwise equality: the run you quoted already measures it. Each arm was also compared against itself, one-shot versus stepwise, same machine, same weights, same dtype. Ours differs from itself by 7.20e-3. The official runtime differs from itself by 7.08e-3, and it has no chunking, which is what makes that second number the informative one. That same official code is bit-identical to itself on CPU; on CUDA it is not, because the `[T,C]` prefill and `[1,C]` decode projections take different matmul reduction orders.

This is not bf16-specific either. On one RTX 5090 with TF32 off, a `[24,2048]` matmul against 24 separate `[1,2048]` ones is not bitwise identical in fp32; each shape reproduces itself exactly across 20 repeats, and the two disagree with each other.

What is answerable is whether the difference is biased or accumulating, which is what the posted run measured: bias of 5.9e-6 additive and 4.4e-5 scale-correlated against a ~9e-3 state deviation, saturating by layer 16 rather than growing.

body:
Hey @Hakureirm, not stale, the bot got ahead of us. The packaging objection from #46984 really is addressed by the `RWKV7-*-20260805` repos, so this is a review call on #47780 now rather than a policy one, and we'll get eyes on it.

One thing worth sorting out meanwhile: the newer `RWKV7-G1j-*-20260831` repos went back to shipping `auto_map` and `modeling_rwkv7.py`, and those are the ones people are actually downloading. If the org can commit to the plain layout for future releases, that retires the last version of the original objection.

Hello @qgallouedec,

The RWKV org added `auto_map` / `modeling_rwkv7.py` to the newer checkpoints to provide broad support in the meantime, as the upstream integration has been pending for a few months(all the tentatives in the past)

If I understand correctly, the `auto_map` implementation is only used when explicitly enabling remote code. Once the native RWKV7 implementation is merged into Transformers, these checkpoints should use the native implementation by default.

So yes, we can move future releases to the plain layout once native RWKV7 support is available in Transformers.
